To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

# Contributing

This repository is a clean-room, MIT-licensed base firmware for the M-VAVE
FM-1 pocket synthesizer (JieLi AC791N). The FM-1's existing community
firmwares are GPL-licensed; ours must be provably independent of them. The
rules below make that provable. Everyone follows them, people and agents
alike. If you are unsure whether something is allowed, **stop and ask the
owner** before you open it.

## Roles

Clean-room work separates the people who have seen the protected code from
the people who write ours.

- **Spec side (exposed).** May read the F-Emulator emulator's source, whose
  chip model was partly written from the hardware layer (`hal/`) of the
  Felucca firmware, hugelton/Felucca, licensed GPL-3.0 (docs/EXPOSURE.md,
  "Corrections", 2026-10-23). Builds the test harness and writes
  `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`: facts only (addresses, bits, pins, timings,
  protocols), never code or code structure, each fact citing a non-GPL
  source where one exists. Never writes firmware.
- **Firmware side (clean).** Writes the firmware. Reads only
  `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, the JieLi SDK (Apache-2.0), FM-1-RE's hardware
  documents (WTFPL), public datasheets, and results of its own black-box
  experiments. Uses the harness only as a command-line tool, and never opens
  `vendor/emulator/` or `harness/` source.

- **Auditor (exposed to the GPL firmwares).** A third role, only for a
  failed similarity audit (docs/AUDIT.md, "When the audit fails"). The owner
  starts one; it works in a folder of its own set up with
  `tools/auditor-setup.sh` (settings `config/claude/auditor.json`), and may
  read the flagged GPL target files and our code. It writes only a finding
  in `audit/findings/`, in general terms (which of our files, the scores,
  the conclusion; never target code). It never writes firmware, the spec or
  the harness, then or in any later session. Its transcript holds GPL
  source, so it is **never archived in this repository**: it goes to the
  owner's private repository `small-beeps-audit` (created, with the
  owner's approval, when the first auditor session runs), committed there
  with an OpenTimestamps proof, and docs/EXPOSURE.md records the session's
  ID, the transcript's SHA-256 and that repository's commit.

Every person and every session is recorded in docs/EXPOSURE.md with its role
and exposure, before it does any work. A firmware-side person or session that
sees forbidden material becomes spec side from that moment: record it in
EXPOSURE.md at once, and stop writing firmware.

## Clean-room rules

### Firmware side never opens, fetches, searches or quotes

- hugelton/Felucca and every fork or firmware built on it (Felucca Salt,
  Felucca 8 Patterns, Hortator, GHOULBOX, Melodee, Skiff, ...);
- zvenson/dinghy and anything built on it;
- the F-Emulator / fm1-emu repository's `fm1-sid/` directory, its
  `probes/lcdtest.c`, and its emulator source (`crates/`);
- any other FM-1 firmware source;
- M-VAVE's stock firmware and any disassembly or function database of it
  (including AL-255/FM-1-RE's `firmware-images/` and disassembly material);
- in this repository: `vendor/emulator/` and `harness/` source (spec side's
  work), and spec-side session transcripts (`sessions/spec/`), which
  contain emulator source. A clean folder never has their contents, not
  even in `.git`: clean sessions run with git's lazy fetching off
  (`GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1`, from `config/claude/clean.json`), so a history
  command that would need them (`git log -p`, `git show`, `git diff`
  across commits) fails instead of downloading them. Give such commands a
  pathspec that leaves the three folders out, and update the folder only
  with `tools/clean-update.sh`. People working in a clean folder by hand
  set `GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1` in their shell too;
- the sites hugelton.github.io and thefirmwarehub.com.

`tools/check-transcripts.py` checks every archived clean-side session against
this list (its `FORBIDDEN` table mirrors it; change both together). Since
M4 it fails a call that accesses listed material (reads, lists, searches,
fetches or checks it out) and logs, report only, one that only mentions it
(sessions/README.md).

### Firmware side may use

Log every use in PROVENANCE.md (an ID, the source, what was learned, where it
was used) and name the ID in the commit's `Sources:` field:

- `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, once it exists (each fact there already cites its own
  source);
- JieLi's AC79 SDK, `Jieli-Tech/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK` (Gitee), Apache-2.0:
  headers, register definitions, drivers. Not its prebuilt libraries;
- AL-255/FM-1-RE (GitHub, WTFPL): its hardware, memory-map, boot-chain and
  update-protocol documents only. Fetch single documents by URL; never clone
  it (a clone puts its firmware images and disassembly material on disk);
- public datasheets;
- our own experiments: test programs run in the emulator, observed only
  through the harness: `tools/fwtest`, whose manual is docs/HARNESS.md;
- answers to spec requests (docs/SPEC-REQUESTS.md), which arrive as facts
  in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.

### Barriers

- **Clean folder.** `tools/clean-setup.sh [DIR]` creates the clean working
  folder: a blob-less clone with a sparse checkout that leaves out
  `vendor/emulator/`, `harness/` and `sessions/spec/` (and marks them
  `-diff` for history commands), plus the Claude Code settings in
  `config/claude/clean.json`, which deny reading those paths, fetching the
  forbidden sites and cloning the forbidden repositories, and turn git's
  lazy fetching off. `tools/clean-update.sh` updates a clean folder and
  checks nothing excluded arrived; C-CLEAN-FOLDER tests all of this in CI.
- **Records in a clean folder.** Each record on the `records` branch also
  keeps the harness's own test results and the hashes of their outputs.
  Records before SR-1-SR-2 also keep the spec experiments' outputs (memory
  dumps, captures, audio); since then a record keeps only their names and
  SHA-256 (`spec-experiments.sha256`), and older records stay as they are.
  Clean sessions never fetch the records branch wholesale (no `git archive`, checkout or
  lazy fetch of a whole record or of the branch): they fetch only named
  files of the firmware's own records, `report.json`, `report.md` and
  named logs under `logs/`, one path at a time. `tools/clean-update.sh`
  also stops if a file under a `harness/` or `spec-experiments/` folder,
  or under the excluded folders, is in `.git` through any branch, the
  records branch included (since M1, after a wholesale fetch brought 17
  such outputs into a clean folder; docs/EXPOSURE.md).
  `tools/spec-setup.sh [DIR]` does the same for spec side with
  `config/claude/spec.json`.
- **One list of the spec-side folders.** `config/spec-side-folders` names
  the three folders once (since M3). The barrier tools build every name,
  pattern and exclusion from it, and their tests use made-up names
  (`tests/helpers.py`), so changing them needs no command that names the
  folders. Scratch test repositories made by hand use the made-up names
  too. The deny lists keep their literal paths (Claude Code's syntax), and
  C-UNIT checks they cover every folder on the list and that no barrier
  tool or test spells one out.
- **Deny lists only grow.** Never remove or loosen an entry in
  `config/claude/*.json`. Check C-DENY-LISTS fails if one is dropped.
- **Session banner.** Both configs run `tools/session-banner.sh` on every
  SessionStart (startup, resume, clear, compact). It prints the role,
  `claude --version`, the SHA-256 of `.claude/settings.json` and of the
  committed config, and the UTC time, and prints `CONFIG MISMATCH` and exits
  non-zero if they differ.
- **Session transcripts.** Each milestone gets a fresh session. At the start
  of every session, before anything else:
  1. archive the previous session's transcript with
     `python3 tools/archive-session.py <transcript.jsonl> --role <role>`
     (it redacts secrets and private paths, writes the copy to
     `sessions/<role>/` and a note beside it). A spec session may archive
     the previous session of either role; a clean session archives only
     clean sessions and never opens `sessions/spec/` (sessions/README.md);
  2. run `python3 tools/check-transcripts.py`;
  3. add this session's entry to docs/EXPOSURE.md.
  A session never archives its own live transcript; the next one does.

content.content:
A session never archives its own live transcript; the next one does.

### Spec-side text discipline

What the spec side learns from emulator source leaves `vendor/emulator/`
and `harness/` only through two doors: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (facts only, each
sourced) and `docs/HARNESS.md` (the harness as a black box). Everything else
the firmware side can read, so spec-side commit messages, pull request
titles and descriptions, and every file outside those two folders and
`sessions/spec/` (docs, tools, tests, records, release notes) describe what
changed in general terms, never emulator internals: no register names,
addresses, struct or function names, or code excerpts. Such detail goes in
comments inside `harness/`. CI logs and records from harness runs show
results (pass/fail, hashes, images, numbers), never emulator source.
`tools/check-emulator-terms.py` (C-SEP-TERMS) looks for identifiers that
occur only in `vendor/emulator/` in all of those places and reports a hit
by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.
Since M4b the terms of the vendored Plaits (`vendor/plaits/`, read only from
its checksum-verified files) are public like the SDK's, the check says how
many emulator terms that takes off, and `vendor/plaits/` itself is not
scanned, except its `SOURCE.md`, which we write (R-SEP-1).

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to
  pass (the `ci` job); no bypass (until 2026-10-22: the repository admin
  role).
- **records-history** (branch `records`): restrict deletions; block force
  pushes; no bypass.
- **records-writer** (branch `records`): restrict creations; restrict
  updates; bypass list: deploy keys only. Together these make the records
  workflow's deploy key the only writer, and it can only add commits.
- **milestone-tags** (tags `m*`): restrict deletions; restrict updates; no
  bypass.

Repository settings: allow merge commits only (squash and rebase merging
off).

Set up on 2026-10-22 by session M0a, with the owner's approval, through the
GitHub API:

| What | ID or fingerprint |
|------|-------------------|
| Ruleset `main` | 25612787 (required check `ci` from GitHub Actions; no bypass since 2026-10-22, before that the repository admin role) |
| Ruleset `records-history` | 25612788 |
| Ruleset `records-writer` | 25612790 (bypass: deploy keys) |
| Ruleset `milestone-tags` | 25612791 |
| Environment `records` | deployments from `main` only; secret `RECORDS_DEPLOY_KEY` |
| Deploy key "records workflow (records branch writer)" | 167260041, write access, ED25519 `SHA256:Od9RfSkzLwqLYSZRf1X7jEdcLhty0n1ISgQ+ec43Dkk` |

The deploy key's private half was generated in the session's scratch
folder, piped into the environment secret without being printed, and
deleted. To rotate it: make a new pair, replace the secret, add the new
public key, delete the old key.

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

## Licences

- Every file we write starts with an SPDX header:
  `SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT` and `SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98`.
  Files that can't carry one are covered in `REUSE.toml`.
- Vendored files keep their own licences (`vendor/*/LICENSE`, `NOTICE`).
- CI runs `reuse lint` and fails on any gap (C-REUSE).
- Never commit the toolchain or anything containing it (docs/TOOLCHAIN.md).
- Nothing secret ever goes in: no keys, tokens or private notes. The
  repository is public and history is never rewritten.

## Privacy

The repository is public. No committed file, commit message or pull request
text names the owner's username, real name, e-mail address, hostname or
local folder names, or a full local path: write paths relative to the
repository, or as `~/...` with the top folder shown as `<top>`. Anyone who
finds such a term in the repository tells the owner instead of repeating it.

- **The terms** are kept by the owner, never in the repository: in the
  gitignored `tools/[REDACTED:host]` (one per line, `#` comments,
  matched ignoring case) and in the repository secret `PRIVATE_TERMS`, which
  CI passes to the check.

  tracked file and every commit message, and the pre-commit and commit-msg

A session never archives its own live transcript; the next one does.

### Spec-side text discipline

What the spec side learns from emulator source leaves `vendor/emulator/`
and `harness/` only through two doors: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (facts only, each
sourced) and `docs/HARNESS.md` (the harness as a black box). Everything else
the firmware side can read, so spec-side commit messages, pull request
titles and descriptions, and every file outside those two folders and
`sessions/spec/` (docs, tools, tests, records, release notes) describe what
changed in general terms, never emulator internals: no register names,
addresses, struct or function names, or code excerpts. Such detail goes in
comments inside `harness/`. CI logs and records from harness runs show
results (pass/fail, hashes, images, numbers), never emulator source.
`tools/check-emulator-terms.py` (C-SEP-TERMS) looks for identifiers that
occur only in `vendor/emulator/` in all of those places and reports a hit
by place and hash, never the word; run it (with `--show`, in a spec folder)
on your commit messages before you push. People review the two doors, so a
term that occurs in either of them as merged on main is accepted everywhere
(read from main's commit, never the working tree: a term a branch adds to a
door is still a hit until that change has merged). Other reviewed false
positives are listed by hash in `config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json`.
Since M4b the terms of the vendored Plaits (`vendor/plaits/`, read only from
its checksum-verified files) are public like the SDK's, the check says how
many emulator terms that takes off, and `vendor/plaits/` itself is not
scanned, except its `SOURCE.md`, which we write (R-SEP-1).

## Commit messages

Every commit follows `.gitmessage` (run `tools/install-hooks.sh` once to make
it git's template and turn on the commit-msg hook):

```
<area>: <what changed, one line>

What:    what this commit does
Why:     the reason (the milestone and requirement IDs it serves)
How:     the approach, and anything tried and rejected
Result:  what the author saw when testing (the CI record is the authoritative result)
Sources: PROVENANCE IDs used (or "none")
Exposure: the author's role and exposure (e.g. "firmware side, none")
```

- `<area>` is lower-case: `docs`, `tools`, `ci`, `firmware`, `vendor`,
  `config`, `sessions`, and so on.
- A field may continue on following lines, indented.
- Agent-written commits end with the trailers `Model: <exact model ID>` and
  `Claude-Session: <session URL>` (and `Co-Authored-By:`). Their author is
  the agent; the owner is the committer.
- Small commits: one idea each.
- Merge commits are exempt from the template; the pull request they merge
  carries the sections.

`tools/check-commit-msg.py` enforces this in the hook and in CI (C-COMMIT-MSG).

## Pull requests and merging

- Agents and contributors commit **unsigned** on branches and open a pull
  request using `.github/pull_request_template.md` (the same sections, plus
  links to the CI run and the record).
- CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) must pass.
- The **owner merges with GitHub's merge button** ("Create a merge commit").
  GitHub commits and signs the merge commit as `web-flow` (shown as
  Verified) and records the owner as the pull request's `merged_by`. No
  squash or rebase merges, and nobody bypasses the rules.
- Records (`records/<sha>/` on the `records` branch) are written only by
  `.github/workflows/records.yml`, for pushes to main, and the similarity
  audit's report beside it (`records/<sha>/audit/`) only by
  `.github/workflows/audit.yml`'s record job (docs/AUDIT.md). Both use the
  `records` environment's deploy key.
- **Performance budgets** (`config/budgets.json`, R-PERF-1) are raised, or
  moved to the next milestone's, only by a pull request of their own that
  says why in the What/Why/How/Result sections and changes nothing else.
  When CI's performance summary shows an improvement of more than 3%
  (R-PERF-2), say so in the pull request's Result.
- Milestones end with a tag `mN`, signed by the owner with their SSH key
  (below), and a GitHub release with the build outputs, the record and an
  SBOM.

### Merge policy and its history

- **2026-10-21:** the owner first chose to sign every merge with their own
  SSH key, as the ruleset's only bypass actor, because GitHub's button signs
  with GitHub's key instead.
- **2026-10-22:** pull request #1 was merged with the button. Its merge
  commit `2fd28219` is signed by GitHub (`web-flow`, verified), and its
  record shows C-MERGE **FAIL** under the old rule ("committer is web-flow,
  not the owner"). The record stays as it is, and history is not rewritten.
- **2026-10-22:** the owner then chose button merges for good. The bypass
  was removed from the main ruleset, so the rules now apply to everyone.

What a merge on main proves: GitHub's signature shows the commit was made
by GitHub on the owner's merge. `merged_by` shows the owner pressed the
button. The required `ci` check shows CI passed on exactly the merged head.
The records workflow re-checks all of this for every push to main
(C-MERGE): a merge commit, a verified signature, committer `web-flow` with
the pull request's `merged_by` the owner (or, for older merges, the owner
as committer), and its second parent the head of a pull request whose `ci`
run passed. Otherwise the record says **FAIL** for C-MERGE, and the record
is still written.

## Rulesets

Repository rulesets (Settings → Rules → Rulesets):

- **main**: restrict deletions; block force pushes; require a pull request
  before merging (allowed merge method: merge only); require status checks to

  pushes; no bypass.

## SSH signing for milestone tags (one-time setup, owner)

1. Create a signing key (or reuse an SSH key you already have):
   `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "small-beeps signing" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing`
2. Tell git to sign with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global gpg.format ssh
   git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_signing.pub
   git config --global tag.gpgSign true
   ```
   Leave `commit.gpgSign` off: merges are signed by GitHub's button.
3. Let git verify signatures locally: add a line
   `<your git email> <contents of id_ed25519_signing.pub>` to
   `~/.ssh/allowed_signers`, then
   `git config --global gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile ~/.ssh/allowed_signers`.
4. On GitHub: Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → Key type
   **Signing Key**, and paste the `.pub` contents.
5. Tag a milestone: `git tag -s mN -m "mN"`, then `git push origin mN`.
6. Check: `git tag -v mN` shows "Good "git" signature", and GitHub shows the
   tag as **Verified**.

# Session transcripts

Every agent session that works on this repository is kept here as evidence.
A session's transcript is the full record of what it read, searched,
fetched, ran and wrote, so anyone can check that a firmware-side (clean)
session never touched forbidden material (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Clean-room
rules"; R-CLEAN-1, R-CLEAN-3).

## Folders, and who archives whom

- `clean/`: firmware-side (clean) sessions.
- `spec/`: spec-side sessions. Their transcripts contain emulator source,
  so `tools/clean-setup.sh` leaves this folder out of clean folders, and the
  clean settings deny reading it.

A **spec** session may archive the previous session of either role. A
**clean** session archives only clean sessions, and never opens, lists or
searches anything under `spec/`. When the previous session was spec side
and the next is clean, the clean session leaves it for the next spec
session to archive.

An **auditor** session (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles") is never archived here:
its transcript holds GPL source, so it goes to the owner's private
repository, and docs/EXPOSURE.md records its ID, SHA-256 and that
repository's commit. `tools/check-transcripts.py` fails on any transcript
outside `clean/` and `spec/`.

## Files

Each role folder holds:

- `<date>-<role>-<id>.jsonl`: the session's Claude Code transcript, one JSON
  entry per line, as Claude Code wrote it under `~/.claude/projects/`, with
  secrets and private details redacted. `<date>` is the UTC date of its first
  entry, `<role>` is `clean` or `spec`, and `<id>` is the Claude Code session
  ID.
- `<same name>.REDACTIONS.md`: what was redacted (kind and count), with the
  SHA-256 of the original and of the redacted copy. The owner keeps the
  originals, so a redacted copy can be matched to its original if that is
  ever challenged.
- `<same name>.subagents/`: transcripts of subagents the session started, if
  any.

## How they get here

A session never archives itself, because its transcript is still being
written. The **next** session, before doing anything else, runs:

```sh
python3 tools/archive-session.py ~/.claude/projects/<project>/<id>.jsonl --role <role> \
    --archived-by "<this session's id>"        # writes to sessions/<role>/
python3 tools/check-transcripts.py
```

and commits the result.

- every transcript must be in the folder of its role (a file outside
  `clean/` and `spec/` fails). When `spec/` isn't on disk (a clean folder),
  spec transcripts are skipped, not read, and the output says so;
- every transcript must show the SessionStart banner from

content.content:
### HW-66: The block moves with a register base, and fwtest
- Fact: a 4-byte instruction moves the registers in a list to or from
  consecutive words at a base register: bytes `xm eb` then a 16-bit
  register mask, low byte first (bit k: register rk, r0 to r15). In the
  first byte, bits 0 to 3 are the base register and bits 4 to 6 the mode;
  bit 7 must be 0 (with it set the bytes are a different instruction).
  The toolchain writes the eight modes as:
  - `0x0`: `{list} = [rN+]`, `0x1`: `{list} = [rN++]`,
    `0x2`: `[rN+] = {list}`, `0x3`: `[rN++] = {list}`;
  - `0x4`: `{list} = [-rN]`, `0x5`: `{list} = [--rN]`,

content.content:
## Instructions

fwtest runs the code the pinned toolchain's compiler emits for the
firmware's flags (`-target pi32v2 -mcpu=r3 -mfprev1`, tools/build.sh),
with the known gaps below. That was checked on a corpus, not proven for
every instruction (SR-7). The corpus: the firmware at `18d9459`, the
vendored Plaits and the demo's C++ built with the firmware's CPU flags,
and several hundred small C functions written to vary types, operations
and pointer patterns, each at `-Os` and `-O2`. Two checks ran in fwtest
0.3.0, each unit on its own:

- every distinct disassembled unit of the corpus's objects (13 981; a
  dual-issue pair is one unit; some are constants in the code, decoded
  as if they were instructions);
- every form in the compiler's assembly output (660, registers and numbers
  abstracted), with each register slot set in turn to r0 to r15 (register
  pairs to each even-odd pair) and each number to values from 0 and ±1 up
  to the 32-bit limits, as far as the assembler accepts them: 34 437
  distinct encodings.

They show only that fwtest decodes and runs each one, not that it
computes what the chip does. An instruction neither check held can still
end a run as a fault ("Outcomes and exit codes"): report it as SR-7 was,
with its bytes and the smallest image that shows it.

Known gaps (fwtest 0.3.0). Each ends the run as a fault, "an instruction
the emulated CPU cannot decode":

- **Rotate by a register.** `rD = rS <> rT` (bytes `cc e1`, then two
  bytes naming the registers), for every register. The compiler emits it,
  at `-Os` too, for a rotate by an amount it doesn't know at compile time,
  such as `(x << s) | (x >> (32 - s))`. A rotate by a constant
  (`rD = rS <> n`, bytes `c4 e1`) runs. Until fwtest runs it, keep rotate
  amounts constant, or hide the amount from the compiler (a `volatile`
  shift count, for example).
- **A 4-byte push or pop of a register list whose lowest register is
  above r0.** `[--sp] = {list}` (bytes `d8 e8`, then the 16-bit mask) and
  `{list} = [sp++]` (`d4 e8`, then the mask), without `rets` or `pc`: for
  example `[--sp] = {r5-r1}` or `{r11-r6} = [sp++]`. Lists that start at
  r0 run, and so do the 2-byte forms and the forms with `rets` or `pc`.
  The compiler was not seen to emit the failing lists (an interrupt
  handler saves a list from r0); hand-written assembly can.

### Block moves with a register base

Since 0.3.0 fwtest runs all eight modes of this 4-byte instruction (bytes
`xm eb`, then a 16-bit register mask; HARDWARE-SPEC.md HW-66). As the
toolchain's disassembler writes them, with n registers in the list:

| First byte | Form | Words moved | The base after |
|------------|------|-------------|----------------|
| `0x0N` | `{list} = [rN+]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x1N` | `{list} = [rN++]` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x2N` | `[rN+] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | unchanged |
| `0x3N` | `[rN++] = {list}` | rN to rN + 4n - 4 | rN + 4n |
| `0x4N` | `{list} = [-rN]` | rN - 4n to rN - 4 | unchanged |

content.content:
- **Q-10. Interrupt details on the chip.** Whether the chip switches
  stacks on an interrupt from user mode exactly as HW-3 says; its nesting
  rules and choice among pending sources (HW-22); whether the two cores
  share one vector table; what `idle` does with interrupts masked (HW-24).
  The toolchain's interrupt attribute works in fwtest.
- **Q-11. Booting on the chip.** The contents of the boot-parameter block
  the loader passes in r0, and whether a raw image can be started on real
  hardware without M-VAVE's loader (PLAN.md, M9 risk), and whether such an
  image can release core 1 as HW-9 says.
- **Q-12. MIDI input.** UART1 and the MIDI jack are not covered here (M6
  will ask).
- **Q-13. The timer acknowledge on the chip.** Whether writing a TIMER0-3
  `CON` to acknowledge its interrupt restarts the count, as it does in
  fwtest (HW-48), or the count runs on and the period stays `PRD` counts.
  The SDK's examples acknowledge every interrupt with such a write but
  don't say. Settled by a probe on real hardware.
- **Q-14. CPU exceptions on the chip.** What the sources don't establish
  about source 1 (HW-49 to HW-51): which causes are on when an installed
  app starts, and which `EMU_CON` and `DBG_EN` bits turn each on (the SDK's
  settings suggest bit n for cause n, but its demonstration reports a
  misaligned access although the SDK never sets `EMU_CON` bit 0); whether
     a heartbeat to RAM on every pass is waiting, by this rule.
   - A read more than 64 cycles after the previous one starts the count
     again, so a loop whose reads are at least 64 instructions apart is
     never treated as waiting.
   - Reads made while core 0 is in an interrupt handler are ignored: they
     neither count, nor jump, nor break a sequence.
   - Reads by core 1 count in the same sequence as core 0's: the rule
     looks at reads of the count, not at which core made them.
   - Other timers' counters, their pending flags, and RAM flags are not
     part of this rule. Polling them never moves time ahead.

**Scheduled events** are what the emulated chip and the script have coming
next:
- the end of a timer period;
- an audio half-buffer finishing;
- a transfer completing;
- a MIDI byte arriving;
- an encoder contact changing;
- a script event.

They count whether or not their interrupt is enabled. **Captures, the end
of the run and the watchdog are not scheduled events:** a jump never stops
for them.

### What that does to captures

- fwtest looks at the board between runs of core 0 instructions. Each run
  is at most 1024 instructions, and no longer than the instructions that
  would reach the next capture (or the end of the run) at one cycle each.
  Captures, the watchdog, halts and the end of the run are checked only
  between runs. A capture is taken at the first such stop at or after its
  time.
- **While core 0 is busy (not waiting), captures are exact:** taken at the
  first instruction boundary at or after the time asked.
- **While core 0 waits, a capture can come late**, because every jump
  inside a run moves time without using up the run's instructions:
A text file, one event per line; `#` starts a comment. Times are emulated
milliseconds with up to three decimals. Events at the same time happen in
the order written.

```
# time   event
2        key 12 down
4        key 12 up
6        key 5 tap 3          # down at 6 ms, up at 9 ms (default hold: 50 ms)
10       enc 0 +2             # encoder 0, two detents clockwise
12       enc 3 -1             # one detent anticlockwise
15       pot 300              # the pot now reads 300
20       midi 90 3c 64        # bytes into the MIDI input, in this order
```

| Event | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `key N down`, `key N up` | Key N (0 to 40) pressed or released. |
| `key N tap [HOLD]` | Pressed, then released HOLD ms later (default 50). |
| `enc N +C`, `enc N -C` | Encoder N (0 to 6) turned C detents (1 to 1000); `+` is clockwise. Each detent is four contact changes, 2 ms apart, the first at the event's time. |
| `pot V` | The pot's reading becomes V (0 to 1023). It reads 900 until a script sets it. |
| `midi HH ...` | Bytes (two hex digits each) arrive at the MIDI input one after another, at the wire's pace: one byte every 320 µs, the first 320 µs after the event's time. |

Key, LED and encoder numbers are fwtest's own. `HARDWARE-SPEC.md` maps them
to the panel and to the key matrix.

## Outputs

All in `--out`. A run writes only what it was asked for, plus
`result.json` and `junit.xml`.

| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| `ram-AAAAAAAA-L-WHEN.bin` | The bytes saved by `--ram` (address as 8 hex digits, length in hex, WHEN as `10ms`, `2.500ms` or `end`). |
| `lcd-WHEN.png` | The screen, 240 x 240, 8-bit RGB, whatever the display's on/off state. Each pixel is the panel's 16-bit colour (5-6-5 bits) with each channel scaled to 8 bits (`c * 255 / 31`, or `/ 63` for green). |
| `leds.csv` | Header `ms,led0,...,led40`, then one row per sample: the sample's time, and for each LED the share of the time since the previous sample (or since the start) that it was lit, in thousandths (0 to 1000, rounded). LED N belongs to key N. |
| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |
| `junit.xml` | JUnit XML: a test case `run` (fails on a fault or hang, and on a halt without `--halt-ok`), and one `golden NAME` per golden file. |

`result.json` holds: `fwtest` (version and the emulator build it carries),
`image` (file name, size, SHA-256), `script_sha256`, `run` (`outcome`,
`detail`, `emulated_ms`, `instructions` per core, `midi_bytes_dropped`,
`unmodelled_accesses`, and every output's name, size and SHA-256), `golden`
(each file's `match` or `mismatch` and why), and `exit_code`.

- `midi_bytes_dropped`: bytes that arrived while the image had no MIDI
  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.

| `leds.csv` | Header `ms,led0,...,led40`, then one row per sample: the sample's time, and for each LED the share of the time since the previous sample (or since the start) that it was lit, in thousandths (0 to 1000, rounded). LED N belongs to key N. |
| `flash.bin` | The flash chip (1 MiB) at the end of the run. |
| `audio.wav` | The audio output: 16-bit PCM, stereo, the header says 44 100 Hz. Every sample the output played, in order. How the firmware feeds the output, and its exact rate: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| `ipb.csv` | Header `block,end_ms,core0,core1`, then one row per audio block (each time the output finished one half of its buffer): its number, the time it finished, and the instructions core 0 and core 1 executed since the previous block (the first row: since the start). Core 0's count is exact; core 1's is counted at a granularity of 1024 core-0 instructions. |
| `console.txt` | The debug console bytes, as written. |
| `result.json` | What happened (below). |
| `junit.xml` | JUnit XML: a test case `run` (fails on a fault or hang, and on a halt without `--halt-ok`), and one `golden NAME` per golden file. |

`result.json` holds: `fwtest` (version and the emulator build it carries),
`image` (file name, size, SHA-256), `script_sha256`, `run` (`outcome`,
`detail`, `emulated_ms`, `instructions` per core, `midi_bytes_dropped`,
`unmodelled_accesses`, and every output's name, size and SHA-256), `golden`
(each file's `match` or `mismatch` and why), and `exit_code`.

- `midi_bytes_dropped`: bytes that arrived while the image had no MIDI
  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.

# Spec requests

How the firmware side (clean) asks the spec side (exposed) for a hardware
fact it needs, and how the answer comes back, without anything else passing
between them (CONTRIBUTING.md, "Roles").

## Asking (firmware side)

Add a request at the end of "Requests" below, by pull request:

- a number (`SR-1`, `SR-2`, ...; never reused);
- the date asked;
- the question: one fact about the hardware (an address, a bit, a pin, a
  timing, a protocol step, a limit), asked as narrowly as you can;
- why it is needed: what the firmware is trying to do, the milestone, and
  what you already tried or read (HARDWARE-SPEC.md sections, the JieLi SDK,
  FM-1-RE's documents, datasheets, your own black-box runs in fwtest);
- the status `open`.

Don't ask how another firmware does something, and don't paste or describe
any material you aren't allowed to read. A question about fwtest's
behaviour (a capture, an exit code, an option) is not a spec request: open
an issue or a pull request against docs/HARNESS.md.

## Answering (spec side)
### SR-3: The panel's wiring and SPI1's set-up on the chip; source 16 in fwtest
- Asked: 2026-10-22, session M2 (firmware side)
- Question: (a) On the chip, how SPI1 must be set up to drive the panel:
  its `CON` bits (mode, direction, enable) and `BAUD` (the clock it gives,
  and the fastest the panel takes), which pins carry its clock and data and
  the panel's chip select, and the `JL_IOMAP` selection and port set-up
  (direction, drive) for them and for PC8 (HW-30). (b) Whether the panel
  has a reset pin and a backlight pin, which, and their levels. (c) The
  panel's place in the controller's 240 x 320 memory (any row or column
  offset) for each `MADCTL` orientation, which orientation shows the
  picture upright as the FM-1 is held, and whether the panel needs display
  inversion (`0x21`) to show colours right. This is Q-6. (d) The longest
  transfer one write of `JL_SPI1->CNT` may ask for on the chip (the
  counter's width or limit). (e) In fwtest: a DMA transfer started with
  `CON` bit 13 clear still raises source 16 at its end, whatever the last
  write to `CON` held (our runs); HW-29 says bit 13 makes a finished
  transfer raise it. Which is right for the chip, and what fwtest does
  for single bytes written to `BUF`.
- Why: M2 brings up the panel and sends whole frames by DMA. In fwtest no
  set-up is needed (HW-29, HW-30), so M2 writes no SPI1 `CON` set-up bits,
  no `BAUD`, no pins, no reset or backlight, and leaves inversion off; it
  sends whole frames as 16-row chunks (7 680 bytes) because only 480-byte
  transfers are confirmed (E-5). Real hardware needs all of (a) to (d).
  For (e), the firmware's handler acknowledges a transfer it didn't chain,
  which is right under either behaviour, but the spec and fwtest disagree.
  Read: HARDWARE-SPEC.md sections 5 and 3, Q-6, the ST7789V datasheet
  (P-11, P-22), and `WL82.h`'s `JL_SPI_TypeDef` and port registers.
- Status: answered in part (HARDWARE-SPEC.md, "12. The LCD on the chip,
  and SPI1 in fwtest (SR-3)"): (a) in HW-55 and HW-56 (SPI1's pin groups,
  the group select, the port set-up registers, `CON`'s named bits, FM-1's
  own `CON` and `BAUD` values) and HW-57 (the panel's clock limit); (b)
  open, the panel's reset timing in HW-57; (c) open; (d) in HW-58; (e) in
  HW-59: the spec is right and fwtest was wrong. fwtest kept every `CON`
  bit once written, so after any write with bit 13 set, every transfer
  raised source 16 whatever `CON` was written to later. Fixed in fwtest
  0.2.0, which `config/fwtest-image` pins from the pull request that
  follows this answer: a `CON` write sets and clears bits as written,
  single bytes in `BUF` follow the same rule as DMA transfers, and a write
  of bit 14 alone also clears bit 13, so acknowledge by setting bit 14
  and keeping the other bits. Open: Q-6, Q-15.
- Answered: 2026-10-23, session SR-3 (spec side)

# Builds everything inside the pinned build container (tools/Dockerfile).
#
#   tools/build.sh image                      build the container image
#   tools/build.sh image-tag                  print its tag
#   tools/build.sh build --out DIR [--src-mount PATH] [--define NAME]...
#                        [--demo plaits]
#                                             build in a fresh container,
#                                             outputs and SHA256SUMS in DIR;
#                                             --define adds -DNAME (test
#                                             builds only, tools/perf.py);
#                                             --demo builds a demo's own
#                                             image instead (M4b: the
#                                             Plaits load test), never the
#                                             firmware's
#   tools/build.sh inside SRC OUT             (runs inside the container)
#
# Builds are deterministic (R-REPRO-3): fixed SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH (set in the
# image), no network, relative source paths with -fdebug-prefix-map, sorted
# output lists, and a check that no output contains the source mount path.
set -eu

ROOT=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)
PLATFORM=linux/amd64

sha256() {
    if command -v sha256sum >/dev/null 2>&1; then sha256sum "$1" | cut -d' ' -f1
                shift 2 ;;
            *) echo "unknown option $1" >&2; exit 2 ;;
        esac
    done
    [ -n "$out" ] || { echo "build: --out DIR is required" >&2; exit 2; }
    tag=$(image_tag)
    docker image inspect "$tag" >/dev/null 2>&1 || cmd_image
    rm -rf "$out"
    mkdir -p "$out"
    out=$(cd "$out" && pwd)
    docker run --rm --platform "$PLATFORM" --network none \
        --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e SB_DEFINES="$defines" -e SB_DEMO="$demo" \
        -v "$ROOT:$src_mount:ro" -v "$out:/out" -w "$src_mount" \
        "$tag" sh "$src_mount/tools/build.sh" inside "$src_mount" /out
    cat "$out/SHA256SUMS"
}

# image and copied to RAM), bss (zeroed RAM, the beacon included), image

### SR-8: MIDI input: the UART the jack reaches, its receive set-up, and fwtest's model
- Asked: 2026-10-24, session M6a (firmware side)
- Question: (a) Which UART receives the FM-1's MIDI input jack, on which
  pin, and the `JL_IOMAP` selection and port set-up (direction, pull-up)
  for that pin. Whether any other MIDI input path exists on the FM-1
  (USB, say), and which path fwtest's `midi` script event feeds. (b) The
  receive set-up for 31 250 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, one stop bit:
  the `CON0` / `CON1` bits that turn the receiver and its interrupt on,
  the flag that says a byte is waiting and how to acknowledge it, any
  error flags (framing, overrun) and how they clear, and the `BAUD` value
  for 31 250 baud from each `CLK_CON1` UART clock choice (HW-53), or the
  formula. (c) The receive interrupt's source number. (d) Whether the
  receiver can be read a byte at a time from `BUF` with an interrupt per
  byte, or only through the DMA window (`RXSADR`, `RXEADR`, `RXCNT`,
  `HRXCNT`, with `OTCNT` as a timeout), how the window wraps, and which of
  the two fwtest models. (e) In fwtest: what set-up counts as "a MIDI
  receiver set up" for `midi_bytes_dropped` (HARNESS.md, "Outputs"), and
  what happens to a byte that arrives before the previous one was read
  (lost, kept, an overrun flag).
- Why: M6a is MIDI in: a byte parser, note and controller messages to the
  FM engine, a receive channel. The parser and the engine's side don't
  depend on the answer and are being built meanwhile; the receiver and
  every fwtest MIDI test do. MIDI out is M6b and not asked here.
  Read: HARDWARE-SPEC.md Q-12 ("UART1 and the MIDI jack are not covered
  here"), HW-53 (the UART clock field), the interrupt and port sections;
  HARNESS.md's `midi` event (a byte every 320 µs) and
  `midi_bytes_dropped`; the vendored SDK's `WL82.h`, whose
  `JL_UART_TypeDef` names `CON0`, `CON1`, `BAUD`, `BUF`, `OTCNT`, `TXADR`,
  `TXCNT`, `RXSADR`, `RXEADR`, `RXCNT` and `HRXCNT` at UART0 to UART2's
  bases, but no bits.
- Status: open
'''
open(p,'w').write(t)
EOF

- Requirements: R-PERF-1, R-PERF-2, R-PERF-4, R-PERF-5 and R-SEP-1
  amended; R-REPRO-7 and R-PLAITS-1 to R-PLAITS-4 new.

  - **Start** (#55): M4's transcript archived; its 3 flagged calls, each
    naming a rule only, approved by the owner. **Neutral rule IDs** (#56,
    the owner's request): the transcript check's rules are `F-1` to
    `F-13`, so naming one no longer flags a command.
  - **The loaded measure** (#57): the perf runs again under a fixed script
    driving every voice and every control (`tests/fw/scripts/perfload.txt`),
    with its own budget, 3% gate and baseline rule, a probe build that
    proves the gate, and `perf-measures.csv` (one row per commit and
    measure; the owner's design). **M4 loaded budget** (#58): 131 072.
    M4's firmware: **114 173 instructions a block** under load, against
    1 813 at rest. Of that, 90% is the panel's drawing (about 66 000 an
    input event), 7% the audio engine, 2% the scan, 1% sending.
  - **Plaits vendored** (#59): 127 files from pichenettes/eurorack and
    stmlib at pinned commits, unmodified, every file MIT; C-PLAITS-PIN.
    C-SEP-TERMS counts its terms as public like the SDK's (the owner's
    decision, with conditions).
  - **The demo** (#61): its own image (`tools/build.sh build --demo
    plaits`), our audio and input APIs only. It needed our own IEEE 754
    soft-float (bit for bit against an exact reference), memory functions,
    six standard headers and two C++ handlers; Plaits builds unmodified.
    C-PLAITS-BENCH measures it in every record.
  - **Spec requests** (#60): SR-4 (the audit: Plaits as base code, spec
    side to make), SR-5 (hardware float on the chip), SR-6 (both cores
    on the chip).
  - **Results** (fwtest, an instruction a cycle; docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md,
    M4b):
    - **Soft-float:** 0.6 to 1.8 million instructions a block per engine,
      2 to 5 blocks' time: only chiptune plays live. Not viable for M5.
    - **Hardware float** (the toolchain's `fprev1`, which fwtest runs and
      the SDK's builds use; SR-5 open): 10 600 to 52 600 a block, 6 to 32
      voices an engine on core 0, the same sound bit for bit.
    - **Core 1** starts and renders a second voice: two at once take half
      the time (fwtest has no contention; SR-6).
    - **For M5:** an FM operator is at most 40 instructions a sample
      (Plaits' six-op, all-in) against M4's fixed-point sine at 25.6: about
      135 operators on core 0 at rest, 91 under the heaviest input, and
      about 135 more on core 1. Plan for half on the chip.
    - **API before M5:** an engine context pointer, knobs as clamped
      parameters, a deadline the engine can see, core 1 as an API, and the
      screen's redraws coalesced to a frame rate.
  - **Next: M5, the FM engine.** Fixed point needs no answer from SR-5;
    floats would. The demo is not shipped in releases.

### M5: the FM engine (firmware side)
- Status 2026-10-23 (session M5, firmware side, on the owner's Mac): done,
  in pull requests #64 (start), #65 (build flags), #66 (screen), #68
  (SR-7), #69 (budgets) and #70 (the engine).
  - **Build flags** (#65): `-mcpu=r3 -mfprev1` as SR-5's answer says
    (HW-62); the image didn't change. `-mcpu=r3` alone turns the float
    instructions on, so the Plaits demo's own C keeps its old flags.
  - **The screen** (#66): drawn in frames of 16 ms, within a drawing
    budget of an eighth of each audio block (R-LCD-6). **Loaded measure
    114 173 to 15 522 instructions a block, 86% less**; LEDs still set as
    each event comes.
  - **The engine** (#70; docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M5): six operators a
    voice, our own sine and ten algorithms, envelopes per operator and
    for pitch, velocity, an index limit against aliasing; 16 voices, 8 on
    each core, allocation and click-free stealing; mono with legato and
    glide; a versioned patch format (docs/PATCH-FORMAT.md) and nine test
    patches of our own; minimal controls (PRESETS, ALGORITHM, KNOB1 to
    KNOB4, SEL with MONO/POLY). R-FM-1 to R-FM-9.
  - **Tests**: FM sidebands within 0.002 dB of the Bessel functions;
    envelope stages within 0.9 ms; glides within 0.05 semitones; velocity
    within 0.03 dB; stealing without a click; 11 s of the heaviest input on
    all 16 voices without an underrun; identical output on two runs;
    golden WAVs for every test patch.
  - **Figures** (fwtest): about 24 instructions an operator-sample; at

  - **Spec request SR-7** (#68): fwtest doesn't run a two-register load

  - **The similarity audit** passes on #70's commit (no pair flagged,

content.content:
/*
 * SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
 * SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
 *
 * The input layer: every control on the panel, and its LEDs (M3). This is
 * the API the rest of the firmware, and engines built on it, use; keep it
 * small and stable (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md, M3, "The input API").
 *
 * - One event queue, read with input_read(). Each event names a control,
 *   what happened to it, a value and the time it was decided.
 * - Control IDs are named after the panel's printed labels (HW-36). Their
 *   numbers never change; a board wired differently from fwtest (Q-7)
 *   changes only input.c's tables.
 * - input_value() gives a control's present state at any time.
 * - input_led() sets the LED of a button or key, with a brightness.
 * - Since M4, input_read_audio() hands the same events to the audio
 *   engine, from a queue of its own (audio.h).
 */

#ifndef INPUT_H
#define INPUT_H

#include "sb.h"

/* Control IDs. Buttons, then the 27 keys from left to right, then the
 * knobs. The 14 buttons and 27 keys each have an LED. */
#define INPUT_OCT_DOWN   0u   /* OCT- */
#define INPUT_OCT_UP     1u   /* OCT+ */
#define INPUT_FX         2u
#define INPUT_SEL        3u
#define INPUT_ENV        4u
#define INPUT_LFO        5u
#define INPUT_EDIT       6u
#define INPUT_GLO        7u   /* the button; the raised key is INPUT_KEY_GLO */
#define INPUT_HOME       8u
#define INPUT_SAVE       9u
#define INPUT_ARP        10u
#define INPUT_SEQ        11u
#define INPUT_PLAY       12u  /* PLAY/STOP, one button */
#define INPUT_REC        13u
/* Keys: KEY1 is the leftmost, KEY27 the rightmost. The 16 lower keys have
 * no printed label; the raised keys are KEY2, 4, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 18, 21,
 * 23 and 26, and the first ten carry second labels (below). */
#define INPUT_KEY1       14u
#define INPUT_KEY(n)     (INPUT_KEY1 + (n) - 1u)   /* n = 1 to 27 */
#define INPUT_KEY27      40u
#define INPUT_KEY_OP1    INPUT_KEY(2)
#define INPUT_KEY_OP2    INPUT_KEY(4)
#define INPUT_KEY_OP3    INPUT_KEY(6)
#define INPUT_KEY_OP4    INPUT_KEY(9)
#define INPUT_KEY_OP5    INPUT_KEY(11)
#define INPUT_KEY_OP6    INPUT_KEY(14)
#define INPUT_KEY_PIT    INPUT_KEY(16)
#define INPUT_KEY_GLO    INPUT_KEY(18)
#define INPUT_KEY_MONO   INPUT_KEY(21)
#define INPUT_KEY_POLY   INPUT_KEY(23)
/* Knobs: MASTER is a pot, the other seven are encoders with detents. */
#define INPUT_MASTER     41u
#define INPUT_SELECT     42u
#define INPUT_PRESETS    43u
#define INPUT_ALGORITHM  44u
#define INPUT_KNOB1      45u
#define INPUT_KNOB2      46u
#define INPUT_KNOB3      47u

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
"""Runs the firmware's fwtest suite and checks what it captured (check
C-FW-SUITE; R-BOOT-1 to R-BOOT-5, R-CLK-1, R-IRQ-1 to R-IRQ-4, R-LCD-1
to R-LCD-5, and since M3 R-KEY-1 to R-KEY-3, R-ENC-1, R-ENC-2, R-POT-1,
R-POT-2, R-LED-1 to R-LED-3, R-INPUT-1 to R-INPUT-3).

  fw-suite.py --build DIR --out DIR

Copies DIR/app.bin (a tools/build.sh output) to out/fw/app.bin and builds
the test images (TEST_BUILDS: the same source with one SB_TEST_* define
each) to out/fw/<name>.bin, where tests/fw/boot.suite expects them, runs
the suite through tools/fwtest (the pinned image), and then checks:

- every case: the outcome the suite expects, no unmodelled accesses
  (until M5 also that core 1 never ran: since M5 it runs the FM engine);
- boot: the marker; the vector table, every slot (HW-18): source 4 is
  sb_tick, source 16 lcd_spi_done, source 5 input_scan (since M3), every
  other source its own stub in crt0.S, by the ELF's
  symbols; the clock measured at startup: SB_CLOCK_CYCLES core cycles take
  CLOCK_TICKS time base ticks (240 MHz against 24 MHz, HW-11, HW-13); the
  first tick within FIRST_TICK_MS of the start (from the last tick's time
  base, the ticks taken and the shortest interval, since the run itself
  ends late); nothing halted;
- heartbeat (one emulated second; the image idles between ticks, so
  captures come late, docs/HARNESS.md "Time"): at every capture at least
  one of the beacon's two heartbeat copies is consistent, beats ==
  ticks // 24000, and both are when its seq is even (the tick handler
  writes them in turn, DESIGN-NOTES.md M1); the consistent copy's ticks
  are no earlier than the time asked less one tick period and START_SLACK,
  and no more than LATE_MS after it; beats never go back. At the end:
  the last tick's time base lies within one tick period (and START_SLACK)
  before fwtest's emulated end time; every interval between two ticks is
  within INTERVAL_TOL of 24 000 time base ticks (1 ms), and so is their
  spread (jitter); beats and ticks taken differ by at most one; the idle
  wait returned at least once per tick and (since M3) at most once per
  interrupt, and core 0 ran at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions per tick
  (M0's polling heartbeat: M0_IPP per period);
- fault and stray: the halt recorded in the beacon (reason and source),
  and the console line, by golden file;
- badinsn: fwtest's own fault outcome for an undecodable instruction. A
  limit of the harness, not firmware behaviour: no handler of ours runs
  (SR-1).
- heartbeat2 (since M2): the heartbeat's checks again over 2.25 s; with
  heartbeat (1.25 s) its difference is the steady state, which may take
  at most IDLE_MAX_IPT instructions a tick. The idle loop's wakes, stored
  once a second, equal the ticks taken since it began, within one.
- screen (since M2): every pixel of the address pattern (300 ms) against
  its formula; the test screen's border, corners and ramps pixel by pixel
  (800 ms); one heartbeat later (1 500 ms) only the heartbeat's rows
  changed; the beacon's screen and seconds shown at each capture; and the
  three pictures against golden images.
- flood (since M2): a test build that sends whole frames back to back from
  500 ms: every tick interval still within INTERVAL_TOL, far more frames
  than ticks, and the picture still the test screen. Prints how long a
  whole frame takes.

- since M3, the panel (tests/fw/scripts/; docs/REQUIREMENTS.md has the
  limits): the input record after the beacon holds the counters, each
  control's value and the last 128 events, each stamped in time base ticks
  from when main started the time base. Each case's events (control, kind,
  value, never times) are compared with tests/fw/events/<case>.txt, and
  written as events.txt beside its outputs. Latencies run from the
  script's time of a change to the event's stamp, allowing for the time
  base starting anywhere within START_SLACK. keys: every key and button
  alone gives control n for fwtest key n, press and release, within
  KEY_LATENCY; its LED lit while held and dark otherwise (leds.csv), set
  within LED_LAG_MS of its event (the firmware's own measure). chords: no ghost, chatter and a glitch
  debounced, encoders exact with keys held in their columns, the panel
  screen against its golden image. encoders: slow detents within
  ENC_LATENCY, exact positions after fast, shared-column and all-at-once
  turns, and every tick interval within INTERVAL_TOL meanwhile. pot:
  steps within POT_FIRST and POT_SETTLED, one way each, no events at rest
  with noise, a rising sweep to 1023. leds (a test build): every LED at its
  brightness step within LED_STEP_TOL. ledshow (a test build, the keys
  script): from input_led to the scan first driving that LED, within
  LED_SHOW_MS (one scan).

- since M5, the FM engine (tests/fw/scripts/fm*.txt; R-FM-*; the engine's
  record follows the audio record; the test patches' values come from
  tools/fm_patch.py): fmbessel, test patch 1's sidebands against
  |J_n(pi/2)| by a least-squares fit at the known frequencies; fmenv,
  test patch 2's stages (each end where its fitted line meets its level,
  its rate, the held level, the attack's linearity, no click); fmmono,
  legato and glide (one sound, one note, the pitch along the glide, no
  new attack); fmsteal, 17 notes on 16 voices, one stolen with no click;
  fmvel, the velocity test build's levels; fmgold and fmgold2, every test
  patch against a golden WAV, twice, the same bytes. audioload is the
  heaviest input on all 16 voices, and checks that core 1 renders. The
  notes case plays test patch 0.

Prints what it saw for the record, and exits 1 if anything failed.
"""

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))

ROOT = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
SUITE = "tests/fw/boot.suite"
IMAGE = os.path.join("out", "fw", "app.bin")
# Test images: name -> define (firmware/src/probe.c).
TEST_BUILDS = {"test-fault": "SB_TEST_FAULT", "test-stray": "SB_TEST_STRAY",
               "test-badinsn": "SB_TEST_BADINSN", "test-flood": "SB_TEST_FLOOD",
               "test-leds": "SB_TEST_LEDS", "test-ledshow": "SB_TEST_LED_SHOW",
               "test-underrun": "SB_TEST_UNDERRUN", "test-velocity": "SB_TEST_VELOCITY"}
# Each case's expected outcome (the suite says the same; checked twice).
EXPECT = {"boot": "completed", "heartbeat": "completed", "heartbeat2": "completed",
          "screen": "completed", "flood": "completed", "fault": "halt", "stray": "halt",
          "badinsn": "fault", "keys": "completed", "chords": "completed", "encoders": "completed",
          "pot": "completed", "leds": "completed", "ledshow": "completed",
          "tone": "completed", "notes": "completed", "audioload": "completed",
          "audiogold": "completed", "underrun": "completed",
          "fmbessel": "completed", "fmenv": "completed", "fmmono": "completed", "fmsteal": "completed",
          "fmvel": "completed", "fmgold": "completed", "fmgold2": "completed"}

MARKER = 0x44304253        # "SB0D", firmware/src/sb.h
TICKS_PER_MS = 24000       # HW-13
START_SLACK = 240          # ticks: 10 microseconds (main starts the time base)
# Startup clears .bss before main starts the time base, at most this many
# core cycles a word (2 measured in M2), 10 cycles a time base tick: since
# M2's frame buffer that is about a quarter of a millisecond, so the slack
# grows with the image's bss (start_slack).
CLEAR_CYCLES_PER_WORD = 3
LATE_MS = 30               # a waiting core 0 crosses many ticks in one run
INTERVAL_TOL = 24          # ticks: 1 microsecond, 0.1% of a tick period
CLOCK_TICKS = (240, 241)   # SB_CLOCK_CYCLES = 2402 cycles at 10 a tick
FIRST_TICK_MS = 2          # the first tick: one period after main starts it
IDLE_MAX_IPT = 1536        # instructions per tick, in steady state (since M2;
                           # 100 until M3's scanning, 1 280 until M4's audio:
                           # DESIGN-NOTES.md, M3 and M4)
SCAN_SLOTS = 12            # input scan interrupts a tick (input.c, since M3)
M0_IPP = 356.887           # M0's instructions per period (its last record)
STUB_SIZE = 2              # crt0.S's sb_irq_stubs
SRC_TICK = 4               # TIMER0 (HW-16, HW-19)
SRC_SPI1 = 16              # SPI1, the panel's transfers (HW-29)
SRC_SCAN = 5               # TIMER1, the input scan (HW-48, since M3)
HALT_STRAY, HALT_FAULT, HALT_STACK = 1, 2, 3

BEACON_FIELDS = ("marker", "beats", "ticks", "period", "seq", "beats_b", "ticks_b",
                 "tick_count", "interval_min", "interval_max", "wakes", "clock",
                 "halt_reason", "halt_source", "halt_reti",
                 # since M2 (firmware/src/sb.h)
                 "screen", "loop_ticks", "frames", "frame_ticks", "render_ticks", "beat_ticks",
                 "shown", "chunks", "wakes_ticks")
BEACON_LEN = 4 * len(BEACON_FIELDS)
CAPTURE = re.compile(r"^ram-01c00000-%x-(?P<when>[0-9.]+ms|end)\.bin$" % BEACON_LEN)
VECTORS = "ram-01c7fe00-200-end.bin"
